screens.title: Deploying Smart Contracts to Ganache with Truffle Migrations
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on migrations, the Truffle mechanism that turns compiled contract artifacts into deployed contracts on a blockchain. You will learn why migrations exist, how Truffle tracks them, and how to deploy a simple contract to a local Ganache network. Think of migrations as version control for deployment: they run in numeric order and persist their history so your team deploys contracts in a predictable sequence. We will create a migration file for a SimpleStorage contract, run truffle migrate, read the terminal output for deployed addresses and gas usage, and then verify the work visually in Ganache. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes such as forgetting to start Ganache or needing to force a redeploy after changing contract code. By the end you will be able to write a minimal migration script, run migrations, and confirm that your contract is live on the local chain.

Deploying with Truffle Migrations

Learn to turn compiled contract artifacts into live contracts on your Ganache development network. Reliable ordering and recorded history are key.

Duration: ~10 minutes demo
In this lesson
Write a migration file for SimpleStorage
Prepare scripts that Truffle will execute in order.
Coming up
Run truffle migrate
Observe terminal deployment details and addresses.
Verify
Check Ganache UI
Blocks, transactions, and the contract address confirm the deploy.
Why this matters

Migrations let teams reproduce the same deployment order and verify addresses across machines. They prevent accidental redeploy order changes and support deliberate upgrades by recording what ran when.

screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives orient your practice with Truffle migrations. First, you will be able to explain what migrations are and why Truffle tracks them. That means recognizing migrations as ordered JavaScript files that persist a migration history so deployments remain consistent across environments. Second, you will create a migration script to deploy a compiled contract, understanding the minimal pattern that Truffle expects. Third, you will execute truffle migrate against a running Ganache instance and read the terminal output to identify transaction hashes, gas used, and contract addresses. Finally, you will verify a successful deployment using Ganache’s Blocks and Transactions views. Each objective is practical: knowing the migration pattern prevents accidental redeploy mistakes, running migrations confidently surfaces deployment details, and using Ganache visually confirms the contract exists on the local chain. These skills together let you manage deployments reliably during development.

screens.title: What are Truffle migrations?
screens.narratorSegment: A migration in Truffle is a JavaScript file that instructs Truffle how to deploy one or more compiled contracts to an Ethereum network. The key properties are order and persistence: files are numbered so Truffle runs them in a deterministic sequence, and Truffle records which migration files have already run so it does not redeploy them repeatedly. This matters because many projects require a specific deployment order — for example, libraries must be deployed before contracts that link them. Treat migrations like versioned deployment steps. A concrete example is the pair of files you typically see: an initial migration that deploys Truffle’s Migrations contract to record history, followed by a second migration that deploys your application contract, such as SimpleStorage. A common misconception is to think migrations are only for production; in fact they are essential during development to reproduce a predictable state, and they make it easy to share deployment steps across a team. Key takeaway: migrations give you repeatable, ordered deployments, and Truffle’s tracking prevents accidental re-execution of the same migration. What are Truffle migrations? means migrations are numbered javascript deployment scripts that truffle executes and tracks to ensure ordered, repeatable deployments.. In practical terms, migrations as ordered, persistent deployment scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › What are Truffle migrations?
Core Concept

Migrations explained

Migrations are scripts that run once in order and are tracked on-chain to prevent duplication.

Ordering
Numbered filenames like 1_ and 2_ determine execution sequence.
Persistence
Truffle records which migrations ran so they are not re-run unintentionally.
Use case
Useful for multi-contract projects and staged upgrades.
Analogy
Think of migrations as commit history for deployments. Each script is a step that can be replayed and tracked so everyone deploys the same set of contracts in the same order.
Key Takeaway

Use numbered migrations to keep deployments ordered and reproducible across environments.

Check your understanding
Why does Truffle track which migrations have run? What happens if order is wrong?

screens.title: Numbering and ordering migration files
screens.narratorSegment: Truffle relies on filename prefixes to determine execution order. Migration files live in the migrations directory and are typically prefixed with a number, such as 1_initial_migration. js and 2_deploy_simplestorage. js. When you run truffle migrate, Truffle sorts files by their numeric prefix and runs each in turn. This ensures that dependencies are deployed before dependent contracts, which is important when linking libraries or seeding initial state. A practical example: always deploy the Migrations contract first so Truffle can record which scripts have executed. A common student misconception is assuming file modification time controls order; it does not. The numeric prefix is what matters. If you need to add a new deployment after the fact, give it the next sequential number. If you must redeploy everything after code changes, use truffle migrate --reset to force all migrations to run from the start. Final check: consistent numbering across teammates prevents divergent deployment histories. Numbering and ordering migration files means truffle executes migration files sorted by their numeric prefix so numbering controls deployment order.. In practical terms, why filenames like 1_initial_migration.js matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Minimal migration script for SimpleStorage
screens.narratorSegment: A minimal migration for deploying SimpleStorage follows a clear pattern. First, load the compiled contract abstraction using artifacts. require with the contract name. That returns an object containing ABI and bytecode Truffle uses to deploy. Next, export a function that receives a deployer object. The deployer is responsible for sending the creation transaction and recording the deployment result. The core line is deployer. deploy(SimpleStorage). Concretely, the file content looks like the two-line pattern where you require the contract and call deployer. deploy inside module. exports. A student mistake is to pass a file path rather than the contract name to artifacts. require, or to forget module. exports entirely. Another subtle point: the migration file must be saved inside the project's migrations directory with a numeric prefix. Example: create migrations/2_deploy_simplestorage. js, paste the pattern, then run truffle migrate. This pattern keeps deployment code minimal and readable. After running migrations you will see a deployed address that identifies the contract on Ganache. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Migration script
Definition

Minimal migration pattern

Load the artifact, export a deployer function, and call deployer.deploy.

// migrations/2_deploy_simplestorage.js
const SimpleStorage = artifacts.require("SimpleStorage");

module.exports = function (deployer) {
  deployer.deploy(SimpleStorage);
};
Concrete example
This file tells Truffle to deploy SimpleStorage and save the deployed address in its migration history.
Common mistake
Using a file path or wrong contract name in artifacts.require will prevent Truffle from locating the compiled abstraction.
Key Takeaway

Keep migrations simple: require the contract by name and call deployer.deploy for a predictable deployment.

screens.title: What artifacts.require does
screens.narratorSegment: The artifacts. require function is how Truffle gives migration scripts access to compiled contract artifacts. When you write artifacts. require("SimpleStorage"), Truffle looks up the compiled JSON artifact produced by compilation and returns an abstraction that includes the contract’s ABI, bytecode, and metadata. This abstraction is what deployer. deploy uses to create the contract on-chain. A concrete example: after compiling, you will have a SimpleStorage. json artifact; artifacts. require points to its exported data by contract name. A frequent misconception is to expect artifacts. require to accept file paths — instead it takes the contract name as defined in the Solidity source. If artifacts. require fails to find a contract, check that the contract compiled successfully and that the name matches exactly. Remember that artifacts. require provides the runtime information Truffle needs to encode constructor parameters and to send the creation transaction. This function is central to the migration pattern because it connects compile-time outputs to runtime deployment steps. What artifacts.require does means artifacts.require returns the compiled contract abstraction (abi and bytecode) that truffle uses to deploy contracts.. In practical terms, loading the compiled contract abstraction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › artifacts.require
Definition

What it returns

An abstraction with ABI, bytecode, and deployment metadata used by Truffle.

ABI and bytecode
Needed to encode constructor arguments and send the creation transaction.
Naming
Pass the contract name exactly as declared in Solidity, not a file path.
Concrete scenario
You compile SimpleStorage, then in the migration you call artifacts.require("SimpleStorage") and pass that abstraction to deployer.deploy. Truffle then sends a transaction that creates the contract and records its address.
Key Takeaway

Use artifacts.require with the contract name to bridge compilation output and runtime deployment.

screens.title: The deployer object and deployer.deploy
screens.narratorSegment: The deployer object is injected into migration functions by Truffle to manage contract deployments. When you receive deployer as the function argument, you can call deployer. deploy with a contract abstraction and optional constructor arguments to instruct Truffle to create a contract on the configured network. Truffle handles the transaction details: selecting an account, estimating gas, broadcasting the transaction, waiting for confirmation, and then saving deployment artifacts. A concrete example is deployer. deploy(SimpleStorage) in a migration file — Truffle uses the compiled bytecode and sends a contract creation transaction to Ganache, which mines a block and returns a contract address. A common misconception is expecting deployer. deploy to immediately return the deployed address; instead Truffle logs deployment status and writes the final address into its artifacts and migration history once mining completes. Use deployer when you need to manage deployment order or pass constructor parameters; otherwise the simple deployer. deploy call is sufficient for standard deployments. The deployer object and deployer.deploy means the deployer orchestrates contract creation: it sends transactions, waits for confirmations, and records deployed addresses.. In practical terms, how truffle sends creation transactions and records results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Deployer object
Core Concept

What the deployer does

deployer.deploy sends contract creation transactions and records results in Truffle’s artifacts.

Transaction orchestration
Handles gas, account selection, and confirmation waits.
Recording
Saves the deployed address and writes migration progress.
Example
deployer.deploy(SimpleStorage) sends the creation transaction and after mining you will see a contract address logged in the terminal and saved by Truffle.
Common misconception

deployer.deploy does not instantly return an address; it completes after the transaction is mined and Truffle records the artifact.

screens.title: Running truffle migrate
screens.narratorSegment: Running truffle migrate executes migration scripts against the network configured in truffle-config, which for a local dev setup points to Ganache. When you run the command from your project root, Truffle compiles any changed contracts, sorts the migrations by number, and runs only the pending ones. In the terminal you will see a step-by-step log: network name and id, each migration file name, deployment steps such as transaction hash, block number, contract address, account used, gas used, and total gas cost. A concrete terminal output example shows two migrations being deployed and their gas costs; importantly it prints the contract address for SimpleStorage — that address is your handle for interacting with the deployed contract. Common issues include Truffle reporting it could not connect to the network; this usually means Ganache is not running or truffle-config points to the wrong port. Another practical tip: if you modify a contract after a deploy and want the new bytecode on-chain, run truffle migrate --reset to force all migrations to run again. That will produce new addresses for the redeployed contracts. Running truffle migrate means truffle migrate compiles, runs pending migrations, and outputs transaction details and deployed addresses in the terminal.. In practical terms, terminal demo: what to expect and how to read output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Running truffle migrate
Process Flow

Execute migrations and read output

truffle migrate compiles, runs pending migrations, and logs deployment details you can verify.

Starting migrations...
> Network name: 'development'
1_initial_migration.js
  Deploying 'Migrations' ...
  > transaction hash: 0x...
  > contract address: 0x...
2_deploy_simplestorage.js
  Deploying 'SimpleStorage' ...
  > transaction hash: 0x...
  > contract address: 0x...
Look for the contract address line — that is where your deployed contract lives on the local chain.
Troubleshooting
If you see a "Could not connect to the network" error, confirm Ganache is running and truffle-config points to the right host and port.
Tip

screens.title: Verify deployment in Ganache
screens.narratorSegment: After running migrations, visually inspect Ganache to confirm a successful deploy. First, open the Blocks tab — you should see new blocks mined that correspond to contract creation transactions. Each block entry relates to a transaction listed in the Transactions tab. In Transactions, look for entries that indicate contract creation; these entries include the transaction hash and the contract address. That address should match the contract address printed by Truffle in the terminal. Check the account list: the deploying account’s balance will have decreased by the gas cost used for deployment. A common oversight is trusting only the terminal output; using Ganache’s UI provides confirmation that the transactions actually mined and that the chain state reflects the deploy. If you don’t see new blocks or transactions, it usually means Ganache was not running when you executed migrations or that truffle-config targeted a different network. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: Two common issues occur during migration work: inability to connect to Ganache and failing to redeploy updated contracts. If Truffle reports that it cannot connect to the network, first ensure Ganache Desktop is running and that truffle-config points to the same host and port. Check that the network name matches the development network used by Ganache. The second common issue happens after you change contract code: simply running truffle migrate will often not update already-run migrations because Truffle records which migration files have executed. If you need the new bytecode on-chain, you must force re-running all migrations with truffle migrate --reset. That redeploys all contracts and assigns new addresses, which is expected since contract code is immutable once deployed. Avoid trying to 'edit' a deployed contract in place; instead redeploy and update any references to the new address. Another frequent developer mistake is syntax errors in migration scripts — these cause immediate failures, so confirm compilation succeeds before migrating. Always recompile after code changes and before migrating. In this lesson we focus on migrations, the Truffle mechanism that turns compiled contract artifacts into deployed contracts on a blockchain. You will learn why migrations exist, how Truffle tracks them, and how to deploy a simple contract to a local Ganache network. Think of migrations as version control for deployment: they run in numeric order and persist their history so your team deploys contracts in a predictable sequence. We will create a migration file for a SimpleStorage contract, run truffle migrate, read the terminal output for deployed addresses and gas usage, and then verify the work visually in Ganache. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes such as forgetting to start Ganache or needing to force a redeploy after changing contract code. By the end you will be able to write a minimal migration script, run migrations, and confirm that your contract is live on the local chain.

These learning objectives orient your practice with Truffle migrations. First, you will be able to explain what migrations are and why Truffle tracks them. That means recognizing migrations as ordered JavaScript files that persist a migration history so deployments remain consistent across environments. Second, you will create a migration script to deploy a compiled contract, understanding the minimal pattern that Truffle expects. Third, you will execute truffle migrate against a running Ganache instance and read the terminal output to identify transaction hashes, gas used, and contract addresses. Finally, you will verify a successful deployment using Ganache’s Blocks and Transactions views. Each objective is practical: knowing the migration pattern prevents accidental redeploy mistakes, running migrations confidently surfaces deployment details, and using Ganache visually confirms the contract exists on the local chain. These skills together let you manage deployments reliably during development.

These objectives emphasize hands-on skill building. You will practice creating a migration file named with a numeric prefix so Truffle runs it in order, and you will use artifacts. require to load the compiled contract abstraction that includes ABI and bytecode. You will run truffle migrate while Ganache is running, observe deployment details such as transaction hashes and gas costs, and take note of the contract address that identifies the deployed contract on the local chain. Finally, you will troubleshoot two common mistakes: forgetting to start Ganache and failing to force a redeploy after contract changes. Practicing these steps helps you develop reliable deployment habits that avoid surprising immutable behavior on the blockchain. Each objective is verifiable by seeing the contract address in the terminal and the corresponding entries in Ganache’s Blocks and Transactions panels.

A migration in Truffle is a JavaScript file that instructs Truffle how to deploy one or more compiled contracts to an Ethereum network. The key properties are order and persistence: files are numbered so Truffle runs them in a deterministic sequence, and Truffle records which migration files have already run so it does not redeploy them repeatedly. This matters because many projects require a specific deployment order — for example, libraries must be deployed before contracts that link them. Treat migrations like versioned deployment steps. A concrete example is the pair of files you typically see: an initial migration that deploys Truffle’s Migrations contract to record history, followed by a second migration that deploys your application contract, such as SimpleStorage. A common misconception is to think migrations are only for production; in fact they are essential during development to reproduce a predictable state, and they make it easy to share deployment steps across a team.
